content: 1. For individuals living with HIV who are severely immunocompromised, the Xpert MTB/RIF assay is recommended as the initial diagnostic test for suspected multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) or HIV-associated TB. This recommendation is based on high-quality evidence for adults and very low-quality evidence for children. 2. The Xpert MTB/RIF assay should also be used as the preferred initial diagnostic test for cerebrospinal fluid specimens in patients suspected of having TB meningitis. This recommendation is supported by very low-quality evidence. 3. For non-respiratory specimens, such as lymph nodes or other tissues, the Xpert MTB/RIF assay may replace conventional microscopy, culture, or histopathology for diagnosing extrapulmonary TB. This is a conditional recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 4. Urine lateral flow (LF)-LAM testing should not be used for diagnosing TB in people with HIV, except in specific cases involving individuals with low CD4 counts or those who are seriously ill. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 5. LF-LAM should not be used as a screening test for active TB. This is also a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 6. TB patients with known HIV-positive status or those living in HIV-prevalent settings should receive at least six months of a rifampicin-containing treatment regimen. Daily dosing is optimal during both the intensive and continuation phases of treatment. 7. Seriously ill patients are defined as those with any of the following danger signs: respiratory rate >30/min, temperature >39°C, heart rate >120/min, or inability to walk unaided. 8. For adults and children living with HIV who are suspected of having TB, the Xpert MTB/RIF assay should be used as the initial diagnostic test. This is particularly important for cerebrospinal fluid analysis in cases of suspected TB meningitis. 9. In settings where TB diagnostic services are unavailable, clinical judgment should guide presumptive TB treatment for seriously ill individuals. Diagnostic confirmation should be pursued as soon as possible after initiating treatment. 10. Extrapulmonary TB is more common in people living with HIV, especially those with low CD4 counts. It often presents as disseminated disease and carries a high risk of rapid clinical deterioration and death. 11. Common forms of extrapulmonary TB include lymph node TB (especially in the neck or underarms), pleural TB (often with one-sided pleural effusion), and disseminated TB. Less common but more fatal forms include pericardial and meningeal TB. 12. Diagnosing extrapulmonary TB is challenging due to the low sensitivity of smear microscopy and difficulties in obtaining samples from extrapulmonary sites. Whenever possible, specimens from extrapulmonary sites should be collected for testing. 13. For suspected TB meningitis, the Xpert MTB/RIF assay is the preferred initial diagnostic test for cerebrospinal fluid. For suspected lymphadenitis, Xpert MTB/RIF may be used on samples obtained from lymph node biopsies or fine-needle aspirations. 14. LF-LAM testing may assist in diagnosing active TB in HIV-positive adults with low CD4 counts, particularly in inpatient settings or for those with danger signs. 15. Presumptive TB treatment should be initiated for patients with danger signs in peripheral health facilities where diagnostic infrastructure is limited. This approach is based on clinical algorithms and expert opinion. 16. Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in TB patients living with HIV is critical for reducing mortality. ART should be started as soon as possible after TB treatment initiation. 17. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). 18. IPT should be provided to individuals with HIV regardless of their degree of immunosuppression, ART status, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy status. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. 19. Children living with HIV who do not have poor weight gain, fever, or current cough are unlikely to have active TB. Those with these symptoms or a history of contact with a TB case should be evaluated for TB and other conditions. 20. If TB is ruled out in children living with HIV, they should be offered IPT regardless of their age. This is a strong recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 21. Children over 12 months of age who are unlikely to have active TB based on symptom screening and have no contact with a TB case should receive six months of IPT as part of comprehensive HIV care. 22. For children under 12 months of age, IPT should only be given if they have had contact with a TB case and active TB has been ruled out through evaluation. 23. All children living with HIV who have successfully completed TB treatment should receive an additional six months of IPT. 24. Isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) with 300 mg daily has been shown to prevent the progression of latent TB infection to active disease. The combined use of IPT and ART provides both TB prevention and mortality benefits, even in individuals with higher CD4 counts. 25. Tuberculin skin testing (TST) should not be a prerequisite for initiating IPT in people with HIV. Those with unknown TST status should be started on IPT after symptom-based TB screening.
